source: Patel (2026) Supersede: Diagnosing and Training the Memory-Update Gap in LLM Agents
finding: When an LLM rewrites a small notes memory after each session, it loses to reading the full history on questions about changed facts. A stronger model narrows the gap but does not close it.
numbers: LongMemEval knowledge-update, oracle split, n=78, LLM judge. Full context vs bounded memory (300 characters): gpt-4.1-mini 82 vs 63 percent (McNemar p=0.0035; 19 vs 4 discordant); gpt-4.1 91 vs 64; gpt-5.4 (low reasoning) 92 vs 77 (p=0.0033; 13 vs 1). Synthetic templated updates with full history: 100 percent for frontier models.
quote: The bottleneck is therefore memory maintenance, not comprehension, and it is not closed by a stronger model.
limits: Memory is rewritten by the model, not by a code rule. So this does not test a code-side replace rule. One benchmark, small n, a 300-character cap is very tight. Preprint, under review, single author.
agent_relevance: The model-written notes lose facts or keep stale ones, so a model-side supersede step has a real cost (G7). A code-side rule is untested here. Clean templated updates are solved with full history, so fan tests must use implicit, paraphrased updates.

source: Patel (2026) Supersede, scale study and training result
finding: Growing the history 24 times at fixed memory size collapses update accuracy. Giving the memory 24 times more room does not bring it back.
numbers: gpt-4.1-mini, n=25, programmatic matcher: 2 sessions with 300 characters 68 percent; 48 sessions (122k tokens) with 300 characters 28 percent (p=0.002); 48 sessions with 7,150 characters 28 percent (helped 4, hurt 4; all 25 answers changed). GRPO on Qwen2.5-3B: 9.0 to 16.7 percent on the n=78 oracle set (single run).
limits: n=25 is small; 'no recovery' means not detected, not proven absent. Single training seed.
agent_relevance: More room for notes did not fix stale-fact trouble; the count of competing versions in the history matters. Supports a supersede rule that removes old versions, not a bigger library. Evidence is thin, so Gap 2 stays open.

source: Brouillette, Kagabo, Faghihi, Ghazzali (2026) Finding the Right Balance: Relevance and Diversity in LLM Retrieval
finding: On clean candidate pools, diversifying the top-k (MMR, Maxmin, DPP) lowers relevance, coverage and answer quality. The best amount of diversification there is about none.
numbers: HotpotQA, bge-m3, k=5, 5,924 test queries, 3 seeds. k-NN S-Recall@5 78.7, EM 50.8, F1 63.6. Classic diversifiers lose 0.7 to 33.0 S-Recall points, all significant (mildest, MMR lambda 0.9: CI -1.05 to -0.54). Tuned RNG-Score +0.2 points, not significant after Holm correction. Reader for EM and F1 is a 27B instruction model.
quote: diversification harms relevance, evidence coverage and answer quality on clean pools
limits: Multi-document QA, not note lookup under one cue. Candidate pools come from Wikipedia-style corpora, which are low in redundancy. Sweeps use injected sentence-shuffled copies. Preprint dated 7 Oct 2026.
agent_relevance: Do not add a dedupe or diversity step by default. It costs relevance on clean pools. This bears on Gap 4 (near-duplicates removed vs left in).

source: Brouillette et al. (2026) Finding the Right Balance, redundancy sweep and answer quality
finding: Once the pool holds many near-duplicates and the query needs several distinct pieces, plain top-k collapses and diversification pays. A rule that diversifies only when the top-k has fewer distinct documents than the query needs captures most of the gain.
numbers: Crossover at a measured near-duplicate pair fraction of about 0.0012 to 0.0030 (cosine above 0.95). Generation with flan-t5-base: on clean pools MMR costs 3.1 EM points (CI -4.0 to -2.3); under redundancy k-NN answer quality collapses. Frozen rule vs k-NN at heaviest redundancy: +22.5 (Qwen3-Embedding-4B), +13.6 (MiniLM), +24.1 (k=10), +21.5 (MuSiQue); at clean levels -0.2 to -1.7. Single-hop SciFact stays flat. An oracle finds a better method on only 5.8 percent of clean HotpotQA queries but on over half when redundancy is maximal.
limits: The transfer tables use the gold count of evidence pieces (oracle analysis). Small reader (flan-t5-base) in the sweep. Not an LLM agent loop.
agent_relevance: Dedupe or diversify only when the candidate pool is measurably redundant and the task needs several distinct notes. For single-note lookup, keep plain top-k. Measure the near-duplicate fraction in the library first.

source: Hu, Zhu, Zhao, Liang, Yan, He, Gui (2026) Beyond RAG for Agent Memory: Retrieval by Decoupling and Aggregation (xMemory)
finding: Agent memory holds many near-duplicate spans, so flat top-k returns repeats. Splitting history into components, grouping them, and retrieving top-down (groups first, raw text only if needed) beat flat top-20 and several memory systems with fewer tokens.
numbers: LoCoMo, BLEU/F1 average, tokens per query. Qwen3-8B: full memory 25.83/33.54 at 18,536; naive RAG top-20 27.95/36.48 at 8,633; Nemori 31.44/40.88 at 7,755; xMemory 34.48/43.98 at 4,711. GPT-5 nano: Nemori 36.65/48.17 at 9,155; xMemory 38.71/50.00 at 6,581. Llama-3.1-8B: xMemory 24.73/34.77 at 5,540. Ablation (Qwen3-8B): decoupled units with plain similarity 31.81/40.77 at 7,236; add group selection 32.55/40.64 at 6,321. Multi-hop 2-hit and multi-hit blocks 13.14 and 12.19 percent vs 7.82 and 6.53 for naive RAG.
quote: flat top-k similarity retrieval often returns redundant context
limits: A whole pipeline changed at once (segmenting, grouping, expansion), so grouping alone is not isolated. Two datasets; readers are small or mini models. Preprint v4, May 2026.
agent_relevance: This is the nearest LLM test of 'group notes under sub-cues' (Gap 3), and it is positive for tokens and quality. But decoupling gave most of the early gain, and group selection alone was flat on F1. Treat as supporting, not proof.

source: Hu et al. (2026) xMemory, group size cap sweep and Fano argument
finding: The number of components allowed per group was swept. A cap of 12 gave the best score; larger groups (14) and smaller groups (8, 10) were worse. This is a small fan-per-group curve for an LLM reader.
numbers: LoCoMo, Qwen3-8B, average BLEU/F1: cap 14 33.19/42.10 (383 groups, 7.47 components per group); cap 12 34.48/43.98 (642 groups, 4.48); cap 10 33.23/42.80 (805 groups, 3.64); cap 8 32.13/41.21 (1,111 groups, 2.58). The authors derive a cap near 12 from a Fano bound with an assumed 2 bits of routing signal, then report that the sweep agrees.
limits: The 2-bit assumption is a modelling choice, so the match to 12 is partly post hoc. Differences are 1 to 2.4 points, no confidence intervals. One reader model.
agent_relevance: Suggests keeping each cue's group small (about 4 to 5 notes on average, hard cap near 12) and splitting beyond that. Same direction as the human fan cost. Needs a replication on a frontier model (Gap 1, Gap 3).

source: Hu et al. (2026) xMemory, uncertainty-guided expansion (Stage II)
finding: After a compact first pass, the system adds raw segments or messages only if that lowers the reader's uncertainty. Uncertainty is the entropy of the next-token answer distribution, or a proxy open model's entropy when the reader hides logits.
numbers: LoCoMo, Qwen3-8B average BLEU/F1 and tokens: decoupled units with similarity only 31.81/40.77 at 7,236; add Stage II expansion 33.23/42.55 at 6,557 (+1.42 BLEU, +1.78 F1, 679 fewer tokens); full system 34.48/43.98 at 4,711. For GPT-5 nano, uncertainty was estimated with a GPT-4.1-mini proxy.
limits: Stage II is mixed with other changes in the full system. Proxy entropy for closed models is an extra call. No calibration curve shown. Greedy decoding.
agent_relevance: Evidence that an answer-probability trigger for a second lookup can work on open 8B readers and save tokens (Gap 7). For a closed API model without logprobs, a proxy model is needed, which adds cost.

source: Moskvoretskii et al. (2025) Adaptive Retrieval without Self-Knowledge? Bringing Uncertainty Back Home
finding: Across 35 methods (8 adaptive-retrieval pipelines and 27 uncertainty estimators) and 6 QA datasets, simple uncertainty estimates decide when to retrieve about as well as complex pipelines, at much lower cost. They still fall short of an oracle that knows when retrieval is needed.
numbers: LLaMA 3.1-8B-instruct main model, 6 datasets (NQ, SQuAD, TriviaQA, 2Wiki, HotpotQA, MuSiQue), 10 metrics. Uncertainty methods use under one retriever call and 2 or fewer LM calls per question. Out-of-domain loss typically under 4 percent. Spearman 0.65 between in-accuracy rank and ROC-AUC rank. Many methods are over- or under-confident.
quote: uncertainty estimation techniques often outperform complex pipelines in terms of efficiency and self-knowledge, while maintaining comparable QA performance
limits: One main 8B model (plus a 72B check). Questions are single-answer QA, not note lookup under a crowded cue. A gap to the oracle remains.
agent_relevance: Supports using answer-token uncertainty as a cheap trigger for a second lookup, but only with an open model that exposes probabilities, and with calibration per task. Does not test crowded cues, so Gap 7 is only partly closed.

source: Yang (2026) Control-Plane Placement Shapes Forgetting: An Architectural Study of Agent Memory Across Thirteen System Configurations (FORGETEVAL)
finding: Code-only supersede, release and purge primitives handle lexical and temporal updates well, but fail when the same cue is written in another form. An LLM at write time or in a mutation hook fixes most of that, for about 17 cents per 385 cases.
numbers: 385 adversarial cases, 10 categories, substring scoring. Deterministic stores (LETHE, LangMem) 70.1 to 70.7 percent on 345 cases; Mem0 76.2. Per category for LETHE: temporal_qualifier 37/37, recursive_supersession 36/39, substring_trap 33/36, identifier_obfuscation 2/38 (5 percent), cross_lingual_id 0/38. LLM mutation hook (DeepSeek-V3) 93.3 percent on 345 (91.7 percent on all 385). Latency 2.3 s per case vs 64 to 191 ms.
limits: Tests whether old facts are removed on command, not answer quality at equal tokens. Author-built suite with partial external check. Preprint, single author.
agent_relevance: A code-side 'one live value per cue' rule is cheap and exact only if cues are canonical. Add canonical cue keys in the write path, and use the model at write time to normalise. This bears on Gap 2 but does not measure accuracy at equal tokens.

source: Zhou, Zhou, Han, Xu, Li, Li, Xiong, Wu (2026) Are We Ready For An Agent-Native Memory System?
finding: A study of 12 memory systems found that systems with explicit update or invalidation handle changed facts better than flat long context, flat embedding RAG and some popular extractors. No single design wins everywhere.
numbers: 11 datasets, 5 workloads. LongMemEval knowledge update, substring EM / ROUGE-L F1: Zep 44.4 / 36.8; MemoryOS 35.6 / 32.2; Cognee 37.8 / 34.0; Long Context 20.0 / 18.0; Embedding RAG 20.0 / 17.8; Mem0 15.6 / 17.1; Letta 17.8 / 5.7; SimpleMem 6.7 / 7.4. LoCoMo temporal EM top is MemOS 8.9. Recall@1 SimpleMem 39.0; Recall@5 A-MEM 69.5, MemTree 59.7.
limits: Systems differ in many ways beyond the write rule, so this is not a controlled test of replace vs append. Low absolute scores. Tokens not matched across systems.
agent_relevance: Directional support that stale-fact handling at write time beats append-only stores on update questions (Gap 2). The comparison is not at equal tokens, so the question stays open.

source: Hsia, Shaikh, Wang, Neubig (2025) RAGGED: Towards Informed Design of Scalable and Stable RAG Systems
finding: There is no single best top-k. Some readers keep gaining up to about k=10 then plateau, while others peak at k below 5 and decline as irrelevant passages pile up, sometimes below their no-retrieval score.
numbers: Retrieval depth swept to k=50 on NQ, HotpotQA, BioASQ with BM25, ColBERT, Contriever. FLAN-T5 and GPT-3.5-turbo: improve then plateau near k=10. Llama and Claude-3-haiku: peak at k under about 5, then decline. Rerankers and prompts do not change the reader-specific pattern. Same trends on CRAG.
quote: reader robustness to noise is the key determinant of RAG stability and scalability
limits: Readers are 2023 to early 2024 models (no current frontier model; a subset used GPT-4o). QA over a document corpus, not notes under one cue.
agent_relevance: Top-k should be tuned per reader, with a sweep from 1 to 20 on the deployed model. Do not assume 'more notes is safe'. Current frontier models are untested here (Gap 4).

source: Jin, Yoon, Han, Arik (2024) Long-Context LLMs Meet RAG: Overcoming Challenges for Long Inputs in RAG (ICLR 2025)
finding: With a strong retriever, answer quality rises and then falls as more passages are retrieved. Hard negatives (near misses from a good retriever) hurt more than weak or random ones. Gemini-1.5-Pro resists random negatives but not hard ones.
numbers: One gold passage plus a growing number of negatives; models Gemma-2-9B-Chat, Mistral-Nemo-12B-Instruct, Gemini-1.5-Pro; negatives from e5, BM25 or random. Accuracy generally declines as hard negatives increase; a stronger retriever means harder negatives. A weak retriever gives a steadier, smaller gain. Retrieval reordering helps as a training-free fix.
quote: the quality of generated output initially improves first, but then subsequently declines as the number of retrieved passages increases
limits: Three models, all from 2024. Exact accuracy values are in figures. QA datasets.
agent_relevance: Near-duplicate notes are the hard negatives of an agent library. Random padding is not a valid control for crowding. Put the best note where the model reads best (see K15). Supports the Gap 4 direction but not at current frontier size.

source: Leng, Portes, Havens, Zaharia, Carbin (2024) Long Context RAG Performance of Large Language Models
finding: Across 20 models, more retrieved context helps only up to a model-specific point. The strongest 2024 models keep improving to about 100k tokens; most open models peak at 16k to 32k tokens and then fall.
numbers: Context 2k to 128k tokens, three datasets, GPT-4o judge. Steady gains to 100k: o1-preview, o1-mini, GPT-4o, GPT-4o mini, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Claude 3 Opus, Gemini 1.5 Pro. Llama 3.1 405B drops after 32k, GPT-4-0125 after 64k, Qwen 2 70B holds to 64k. Most open-source models are effective only to roughly 16k to 32k.
quote: only a handful of the most recent state of the art LLMs can maintain consistent accuracy at long context above 64k tokens
limits: Total context length varied, not the number of items under one cue. 2024 models. Failure types (refusal, wrong answer) analysed only for selected models.
agent_relevance: On the best models the cost of extra retrieved text is small within tens of thousands of tokens, so fan costs for a compact library may be smaller than for weaker readers. Still no direct slope for 1 to 50 notes per cue (Gap 1).

source: Gao et al. (2026) The First Drop of Ink: Nonlinear Impact of Distracting Information in Long-Context Reasoning (ICML 2026)
finding: In a fixed-length context, the first small share of hard distractors does most of the damage. Accuracy falls on a convex curve with the share of hard distractors. This matches a log-like cost for the first competitors.
numbers: Natural Questions, TriviaQA, PopQA, HotpotQA at 128K tokens; Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-Next-80B (and others). Drop ratio (loss in the first 10 percent of hard distractors over total loss) for Qwen2.5-7B on nq easy at 128K is 0.58; linear would be 0.1. Attention on the gold passage falls 76 percent when 10 percent of 100 distractors are hard (97 to 21 percent in the paper's example). Filtering helps mostly by shortening the context; recovery needs a hard-distractor share near zero.
quote: performance drops sharply within the first small fraction of hard-distractor proportion
limits: Open models up to 80B, not current frontier models. Share of distractors in a long context, not count of items under one cue.
agent_relevance: Indirect support for K02: the first extra competitor hurts most. For the agent, one near-miss note may cost more than the next three. It is not a fan test. A frontier replication is needed for Gap 1.

source: Chroma Research (2025) Context Rot: How Increasing Input Tokens Impacts LLM Performance
finding: Across 18 models, accuracy degrades with input length even on simple tasks. Needles less similar to the question degrade faster. A single distractor lowers accuracy and some distractors are much worse than others. Models almost never refuse.
numbers: 18 models (Anthropic 5, OpenAI 7, Google 3, Alibaba 3). Needle-question similarity 0.445 to 0.775 (essays) and 0.521 to 0.829 (arXiv), 8 needles per topic. Distractors tested at 0, 1 and 4. LongMemEval: full prompts about 113k tokens vs focused prompts about 300 tokens, 306 prompts. Refusals 69 of 194,480 calls (0.035 percent). Shuffled haystacks did better than coherent ones.
quote: Even a single distractor reduces performance relative to the baseline (needle only)
limits: Vendor technical report. The page text I read gave directions and design but no accuracy tables; per-model values are in charts. Coherent vs shuffled haystack is not a fan test.
agent_relevance: Supports the idea that models fail silently with a wrong answer instead of saying 'unsure' (0.035 percent refusals), so refusal is not a trigger (K22). Also shows a short focused context beats the full history on LongMemEval.

source: Du et al. (2025) Context Length Alone Hurts LLM Performance Despite Perfect Retrieval
finding: Longer input hurts even when the evidence is retrieved perfectly, when the extra tokens are blank, and when they are masked. Asking the model to recite the evidence first turns a long task into a short one.
numbers: 5 open and closed models, math, question answering and code. Accuracy drop of 13.9 to 85 percent as input length grew within claimed windows. Recite-then-solve improved GPT-4o by up to 4 percent on RULER.
limits: I read the abstract page only. Model names and per-task numbers not seen. A length effect separate from the number of competitors.
agent_relevance: Fan tests must hold total tokens fixed (pad the low-fan arm), or length will be mistaken for fan (K05). A 'recite the chosen notes first' step is a cheap shortening trick to test.

source: OpenAI MRCR dataset card (huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr)
finding: Closest public natural-text test of cue overload: 2, 4 or 8 identical requests (for example, a poem about tapirs) are hidden in a long chat, and the model must return the i-th one. The cue is the same, the answers are similar, and only order tells them apart.
numbers: 438 entities, 10 writing formats, 100 samples per token bin from 4,096 to 1,048,576 tokens. Replies written by GPT-4o. Score is the difflib ratio against the true answer after a required hash prefix; no hash scores 0. The card gives no per-needle accuracy.
limits: Index-by-order, not by content; needle count and context length move together in published summaries. Accuracy tables live in lab blog posts I could not open.
agent_relevance: The right design to copy for Gap 1: vary 1, 2, 4, 8, 16 near-identical notes under one cue at fixed total tokens. No such published curve for a current frontier model was found in primary text.

source: benchmarklist.com MRCR v2 8-needle page (aggregator of lab-reported scores)
finding: Self-reported 8-needle MRCR v2 scores for three recent Gemini models are far from ceiling.
numbers: Gemini 3.6 Flash 54 percent; Gemini 3.5 Flash 26.6 percent; Gemini 3.1 Pro 26.3 percent. Self-reported, sampled 2026-07-21. Context bucket not stated on the page (another aggregator ties 26.3 to a 1M-token pointwise score and 84.9 percent to the 128K average, unverified).
limits: Aggregator, not the lab report. No 2-needle or 4-needle value for the same models on the page, so the fan slope cannot be read.
agent_relevance: Eight near-identical items under one cue is still hard for recent models at long context. Do not rely on the bucket. Treat as a pointer only.

source: benchmarklist.com OpenAI MRCR 2-needle 128k and 1M pages (seen in search results only)
finding: Second-hand launch-post numbers for the 2-needle task at 128K: current OpenAI reasoning models score much higher than GPT-4.1.
numbers: 128K, 2 needles: GPT-5 (high) 95.2; GPT-5 mini (high) 84.3; GPT-4.1 57.2; o4-mini (high) 56.4; o3 (high) 55.0; GPT-4.1 mini 47.2; GPT-5 nano (high) 43.2; GPT-4.1 nano 36.6. 1M: GPT-4.1 46.3, mini 33.3, nano 12.0. Another snippet lists GPT-5.4 97.3 and GPT-5.5 98.1 on 8 needles at 4K to 8K.
limits: Only seen in search result text, not opened. Aggregator, may be mis-copied. Not comparable across dataset versions.
agent_relevance: If true, fan cost at short context is near zero for the newest models and appears with length. Needs the primary launch posts before any decision.

source: Vodrahalli et al. (2024) Michelangelo: Long Context Evaluations Beyond Haystacks via Latent Structure Queries
finding: The original MRCR task places adversarially similar needles in natural writing (poem about penguins vs flamingos, or first vs second poem). It has only two confounders, so it gives fan 2 to 3, not a curve. The authors note it is easy to extend to many more.
numbers: Score is a string-similarity ratio. Gemini models stay flat to 1M tokens after an early drop; GPT and Claude models fall faster. Model families show parallel curves. Latent List chance rate is 12.2 percent on average.
limits: Fixed small number of confounders. 2024 models. Not a fan sweep.
agent_relevance: Confirms that no primary paper I could open sweeps same-cue near-duplicates from 1 to 50 on current models, so Gap 1 stays open.

source: Leviathan, Kalman, Matias (2025) Prompt Repetition Improves Non-Reasoning LLMs
finding: Writing the same prompt twice raises accuracy for non-reasoning models. Padding to the same length does not. With reasoning on, the effect is neutral.
numbers: Gemini 2.0 Flash and Flash Lite, GPT-4o and 4o-mini, Claude 3 Haiku and Sonnet, DeepSeek V3; 7 benchmarks plus 2 custom tasks; 47 of 70 combinations significantly better (McNemar p<0.1), 0 worse. NameIndex (50 names, ask for the 25th): Flash-Lite 21.33 to 97.33 percent. Three copies often beat two on the custom tasks. With reasoning: 5 wins, 1 loss, 22 ties of 28.
limits: Repeats the prompt, not a stored note. Older small models. It is not a test of strength accumulating through successful use.
agent_relevance: Only an indirect hint on Gap 5 and Gap 6: re-exposure of content helps a causal reader, so listing the key note a second time near the query is cheap to test. It says nothing about whether past successful use makes a note safer.

source: Anderson (1974) Retrieval of propositional information from long-term memory (Cognitive Psychology 6:451-474), abstract and design only
finding: Judgment times for probe sentences grow with the number of study sentences that share the probe's person or place. A model assumes parallel access from all concepts and serial search within each.
numbers: Design as reported by secondary sources: 26 study sentences, 16 persons and 16 places, a person is in a place. The per-cell reaction times and error rates were not reached; the UMich copy sits behind a Cloudflare check and the Elsevier copy behind a paywall.
limits: Not opened. No numbers recorded. Do not quote cell values from memory.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open for Anderson 1974. Use the ACT-R summary numbers in a03 to a09 as the working figures.

source: Watkins and Watkins (1975) Buildup of proactive inhibition as a cue-overload effect, and Fujita and Sasakawa test (seen through search snippets)
finding: The Watkins paper argues proactive inhibition builds up because a retrieval cue gets tied to more items, not because older items interfere in general. A later Japanese study tested cue overload by changing list composition and length: 4-item conditions beat 8-item conditions on every trial.
numbers: Crossref confirms JEP: Human Learning and Memory 1(4), 442-452. No recall cells reached; the APA and Springer pages were not opened. The Fujita and Sasakawa figures come from a search summary only.
limits: Not opened. The 4 vs 8 result is second-hand.
agent_relevance: Gap 9 stays open for Watkins and Watkins. Fan 4 vs 8 seems to cost recall in people, which agrees with the log shape but gives no size.

source: Mem0 team blog (2026) token-efficient memory algorithm, ADD-only design (seen through search snippet)
finding: A vendor says it moved from extract-then-reconcile (update and delete) to a single add-only pass and credits that for a +42.1 gain on temporal reasoning at under 7,000 tokens per retrieval. An independent study cited alongside found Mem0's own update path scored 24.7 points lower in one setup.
numbers: Vendor figures: +42.1 temporal reasoning, under 7,000 tokens per retrieval call. Separate study: insertions were 87.6 percent of operations in one system.
limits: Only seen in search results, not opened. Pre/post version comparison, not a single-variable test. Vendor claim.
agent_relevance: A counter-signal to Gap 2: an LLM-run update step can lose facts, so add-only plus read-time handling may beat model-run replace. A code-run rule is a different thing and is still untested at equal tokens.
